title: Motorcycle BrandsUpdated Jul 05, 2026The 20 Best Motorcycle Brands (2026 Edition

contentBlocks.text: With hundreds of motorcycle brands out there, it can feel overwhelming to find the right one, whether you're just starting out or have been riding for years.

Consumer Reports found that while German and American bikes might need more time in the shop, owners actually feel most satisfied with Harley-Davidson and BMW over the long term. Meanwhile, Japan's "Big Four" still dominate the roads with their own strengths. Honda and Yamaha lead global sales thanks to their incredibly strong and reliable frames. Kawasaki, along with Yamaha, builds really fast bikes for those who love speed. And if you want a dependable Japanese bike that's also affordable, Suzuki is often the best choice.
Ultimately, the perfect bike for you depends on where you ride, your personal taste, and how much experience you have.

To help you sort through all the options, we've gathered 20 top motorcycle brands from around the world. Here's an honest look at their backgrounds, what they're known for, and what it's really like to ride them.
1. Yamaha (Japan)
2. Honda (Japan)
3. Harley-Davidson (U.S.)
4. BMW (Germany)
5. Kawasaki (Japan)
6. Ducati (Italy)
7. KTM (Austria)
8. Triumph (United Kingdom)
9. Suzuki (Japan)
10. Aprilia (Italy)
11. Indian Motorcycle (U.S.)
12. Moto Guzzi (Italy)
13. MV Agusta (Italy)
14. Royal Enfield (India)
15. Benelli (Italy)
16. Bajaj (India)
17. Norton (United Kingdom)
18. CFMOTO (China)
19. Bimota (Italy)
20. Hero (India)
1Yamaha

If there is one word that perfectly describes Yamaha, it’s versatility. Founded in 1955 and headquartered in Iwata, Japan, this company doesn't just build motorcycles—they build engines with unmatched personality.

For years, Yamaha has dominated the streets thanks to its brilliant crossplane-concept engine platforms: the punchy twin-cylinder CP2 and the legendary, snarling three-cylinder CP3. Instead of chasing sterile, clinical specs on paper, Yamaha builds bikes that feel alive.

Look at their lineup today, and you’ll find a precision tool for every flavor of hooliganism. If you want a naked street bike that doubles as an absolute wheelie machine, the MT-09 (especially the track-ready SP edition) remains the gold standard. If you want to lose yourself in the backcountry and need a bulletproof adventure bike you can drop all day without breaking, the bare-bones Tenere 700 is legendary. And while strict emissions have tragically forced the iconic YZF-R1 into a track-only retirement, its MotoGP-inspired crossplane wail lives on in the DNA of their sharp new weapon, the YZF-R9.
You buy a Yamaha because you want that legendary Japanese reliability, but you also want a machine that actually knows how to party.
Official Site: www.yamaha-motor.com
2Honda

If there is a global benchmark for motorcycle engineering, it’s Honda. Established in 1949 and headquartered in Tokyo, Honda isn't just the biggest motorcycle manufacturer on Earth—they are the creators of the most refined, bulletproof machines ever built. In the motorcycle community, there is a running joke that you can leave a Honda at the bottom of a lake for a decade, pull it out, change the oil, and it will fire right up.

Honda's philosophy has always been about rideability and perfection. Their bikes might not always have the most aggressive, terrifying power bands on paper, but they are so perfectly balanced that they make every rider look like a pro.

Their modern lineup is packed with absolute legends. If you want the ultimate luxury cross-country tourer, the flat-six Gold Wing is still the undisputed king of the highway. If you want to tackle everything from local trails to a trip around the world, the heavy-duty Africa Twin offers some of the best adventure tech and chassis engineering on the market. And on the flip side, Honda completely rules the lightweight and fun categories with machines like the iconic Rebel cruisers, the trail-ready CRF300L, and mini-moto icons like the Grom and Super Cub—bikes that make riding accessible to absolutely everyone.
You buy a Honda because you want a bike that will outlive you, your kids, and probably the garage you park it in.
Official Site: powersports.honda.com
3Harley-Davidson

Let's skip the marketing fluff: Harley-Davidson isn't just a motorcycle brand; it's a heavy-metal American religion. Born in a Milwaukee shed in 1903, Harley represents pure, unadulterated Americana on two wheels. They don’t sell sterile performance metrics—they sell a rumbling V-Twin lifestyle, heavy iron, and a counter-culture heritage that you can feel in your chest when you twist the throttle.

To be fair, those Consumer Reports surveys aren't lying. If you buy a Harley, you will likely spend more time turning wrenches and dealing with shop visits than you would on a metric cruiser. But nobody walks into a Harley dealership looking for a sensible, logical commuter. You buy into the culture, the chrome, and that classic, low-end torque.

While massive highway-shredding baggers like the Softail and Touring lines still keep the old-school faithful happy, Harley hasn't been stuck in the past. They’ve recently injected some serious modern performance into the lineup with the liquid-cooled Revolution Max engine, giving the aggressive Sportster S some real teeth. Even wilder? They successfully built the Pan America, a highly competitive, high-tech adventure bike that honestly shocked the European market.
Love them or hate them, when a Harley rumbles past on the sidewalk, everybody turns their head to look.
Official Site: www.harley-davidson.com
4BMW

If you’ve ever seen a muddy, heavy-duty bike loaded down with aluminum panniers parked outside a remote coffee shop in the middle of nowhere, you’ve seen a BMW GS. The German giant has been building motorcycles since 1923, and they basically invented the modern adventure touring category.

Their undisputed crown jewel today is the R 1300 GS (along with its massive Adventure variant). It’s powered by that iconic, quirky-looking Boxer engine with the cylinders sticking straight out of the sides. It looks a bit weird, but that low center of gravity and the relentless, shaft-driven power make it the absolute king of global exploration.

But BMW isn't just for riding into the wilderness. On the other side of the showroom, they build the S 1000 RR—a terrifyingly fast sportbike that literally forced the entire Japanese industry to rethink how sportbike electronics and aerodynamics should work.

To be fair, BMWs are notoriously expensive to maintain. Just like those reliability surveys suggest, they have their fair share of electrical glitches that will eventually require some premium shop time. But for riders who crave cutting-edge tech, heated grips, adaptive cruise control, and effortless high-speed travel, nothing else on the road feels quite as premium.
Official Site: www.bmwmotorcycles.com
5Kawasaki
Kawasaki doesn’t care about being polite. While Honda focuses on perfection and Yamaha focuses on versatility, Kawasaki’s entire brand identity can be summed up in one word: Speed.

Draped in their unmistakable, loud Lime Green racing livery, this brand targets the horsepower junkies. Look no further than the Ninja H2 and its track-only sibling, the H2R—a supercharged, carbon-fiber monster that essentially stands alone as a flex of pure engineering madness.

Even in the real world, their lineup is built to weaponize asphalt. The ZX-10R is a multi-time World Superbike champion that offers zero apologies for its back-breaking, aggressive clip-on posture, while their naked Z900 and entry-level Ninja 400 / 500 platforms consistently dominate sales charts by giving street riders maximum acceleration and sharp handling for the absolute lowest dollar amount possible. They are noisy, they vibrate, and they feel a bit raw around the edges, but a Kawasaki will always give you an adrenaline rush the second the tachometer sweeps past 8,000 RPM.
Official Site: www.kawasaki.com
6Ducati

Ducati is the Ferrari of two wheels, period. You don't buy a Ducati with your brain; you buy it because your heart skips a beat when you see that gorgeous Italian red trellis frame. Founded in Bologna, they transitioned from making radio components to building some of the most exotic, loud, and breathtakingly beautiful racing machinery on the planet.

Their modern Desmosedici-inspired V4 engines have completely broken the motorcycle world. The Panigale V4 is pure, unfiltered track pornography, pushing out over 210 horsepower in a chassis that feels as sharp as a scalpel. If you don't want to ruin your lower back on a sportbike, they slapped that same insane V4 motor into the Multistrada V4, creating a high-riding touring bike that can comfortably crush a continent while effortlessly keeping up with supercars in the canyons.

They rattle at idle, they run notoriously hot in city traffic, and the Desmodromic valve maintenance intervals will absolutely torch your bank account. But that is the price of admission for owning a rolling piece of Italian art that screams like a MotoGP bike.
Official Site: www.ducati.com
7KTM

KTM’s corporate slogan is "Ready to Race," and they mean it in the most literal, chaotic way possible. Based in Mattighofen, Austria, this brand started by completely dominating the dirt, building the most violent, lightweight motocross and enduro bikes on earth.

When they decided to bring that dirt-bike energy to the street, things got wonderfully weird. They specialize in ultra-aggressive, angular bikes that look like they were designed by a mad scientist with an orange obsession.

Take the 1390 Super Duke R Evo, affectionately and terrifyingly nicknamed "The Beast." It’s a naked bike with a massive V-twin engine that produces so much low-end torque it feels like it’s actively trying to rip your arms out of their sockets every time you whack the throttle open. Their adventure lineup, led by the 1290/1390 Super Adventure, handles off-road terrain with a raw, aggressive capability that makes smoother bikes feel like street tourers. KTMs are temperamental, their electronics can be finicky, and they always demand 100% of your attention. It is absolutely not a brand for beginners or casual weekend cruisers—it’s for riders who want their bikes to feel just a little bit dangerous.
Official Site: www.ktm.com
8Triumph
Triumph is the master of playing both sides of the coin. On one hand, this Hinckley-based legend owns the retro throwback scene; on the other, they build high-tech, razor-sharp track weapons.

If you want that timeless, Steve McQueen cool factor, their Modern Classics lineup—anchored by the gorgeous Bonneville T120 and the aggressive Thruxton café racers—is pure rolling nostalgia done right. But if you think Triumph is just about tweed jackets and leather boots, twist the throttle on the Street Triple 760 RS or the flagship Speed Triple 1200 RS. These bikes use an incredibly linear, howling three-cylinder inline engine that gives you the perfect middle ground between twin-cylinder grunt and four-cylinder top-end scream. Oh, and if you want to completely absurdly flex on your garage neighbors, they also make the Rocket 3, a cruiser packing a massive 2,458cc engine—the largest production motorcycle motor on Earth.
Official Site: www.triumphmotorcycles.com
9Suzuki

Suzuki is the unpretentious working-man's hero of the "Big Four." They don't update their bikes every two years, and they don't care about flashy, fragile electronics packages. Instead, they focus on bulletproof, analog reliability at a price point that makes European brands look like a total scam.

Take the SV650, a V-twin naked bike that has remained largely unchanged for decades because it is quite literally a perfect motorcycle for both absolute beginners and club racers. Then there is the legendary Hayabusa, a land-missile of an inline-four that defined the 1990s top-speed wars and still commands absolute respect on the highway today. Recently, they finally modernized with an incredibly smooth, punchy new parallel-twin platform inside the V-Strom 800DE adventure bike and the GSX-8S street fighter.
A Suzuki won't make you look like a high-fashion model, but it will start every single morning, take an absolute beating, and cost you pennies to maintain.
Official Site: www.suzukicycles.com
10Aprilia

If Ducati is Ferrari, Aprilia is the raw, hardcore racing outfit that spends all its money on aerodynamics and chassis engineering instead of lifestyle marketing. Emerging from Noale, Italy, with a wall full of MotoGP championships, this brand builds bikes for riders who care about absolute lap times above everything else.

Their magnum opus is the Tuono V4 and its track-fairing twin, the RSV4. Powered by a ferocious, compact V4 engine that sounds like a mechanical thunderstorm, these bikes have what many journalists consider the finest, most intuitive front-end feel in the history of sportbikes. It tilts into corners like it’s reading your mind. For the real world, they recently hit a massive home run with the RS 660 and Tuareg 660, proving they can build lightweight, parallel-twin middleweights that still possess that magical, sharp-handling Italian DNA. They run hot, the dealership network can be sparse, but on a twisting backroad, nothing else carves pavement quite like an Aprilia.
Official Site: www.aprilia.com
11Indian Motorcycle

As America’s oldest motorcycle brand (founded in 1901), Indian has spent the modern era under the ownership of Polaris, staging an absolute street war against Harley-Davidson. And honestly? They are winning over a lot of converts by building bikes that respect old-school heritage while embracing modern engineering.

Their big-bore baggers like the Chieftain and the liquid-cooled Challenger offer a stiffer chassis, better cornering clearance, and punchier overhead-cam V-twin motors than their Milwaukee rivals. But their biggest cult hit is undoubtedly the FTR 1200, a flat-track-inspired, high-performance naked bike that trades traditional American chrome for raw, broad-shouldered asphalt carving.

They offer that distinct, heavy American iron feel, but with a level of tight manufacturing quality that means you spend less time turning wrenches in the garage and more time swallowing highway miles.
Official Site: www.indianmotorcycle.com
12Moto Guzzi

Moto Guzzi is pure mechanical character. Operating out of the same factory in Mandello del Lario since 1921, they are famous for one highly specific design: an air-cooled, transversely mounted V-twin engine where the cylinder heads stick right out to the left and right sides, directly into the wind.

When you start a Moto Guzzi at a red light, the whole bike violently twists to the right from the torque reaction of the crankshaft. It’s an intoxicating, analog feeling that modern, sterile bikes have completely engineered out. Models like the V7 cruiser are the epitome of effortless, shaft-driven retro cool, while the newer V100 Mandello introduces liquid-cooling and adaptive, motorized aerodynamic wings that move based on your speed. It’s a niche brand for riders who want to slow down, enjoy the rhythm of a unique motor, and ride something that feels completely distinct from the sea of inline-fours.
Official Site: www.motoguzzi.com
13MV Agusta

MV Agusta's tagline is "Motorcycle Art," and for once, a marketing department isn’t lying. These bikes are ultra-premium, low-volume exotics designed for people with incredibly deep pockets. Under the fresh corporate backing of KTM/Pierer Mobility, MV Agusta is currently refining its notoriously chaotic reliability while keeping its wild, elite design language intact.

Machines like the Brutale 1000 RR and the triple-exhaust Dragster 800 look like aggressive, futuristic sculptures. They are defined by gorgeous single-sided swingarms, exposed trellis frames, and inline engines that scream all the way to a terrifying 14,000 RPM. You don’t park an MV Agusta in a dusty shed; you park it in a climate-controlled garage next to your sports car. They are twitchy, hyper-aggressive, and wildly expensive to service—but they are easily the most jaw-dropping machines on any motorcycle grid.
Official Site: www.mvagusta.com
14Royal Enfield

Originally a British brand before setting up shop permanently in India, Royal Enfield is currently undergoing a massive global renaissance. They don't make superbikes, and they don't care about high horsepower. Their mission is simple: affordable, dead-simple, charmingly vintage motorcycling.

They shook up the global market with their 650cc twin platform found in the Interceptor 650 and Continental GT, giving riders authentic, 1960s British twin styling and solid reliability for a fraction of the price of a Triumph. For the adventure crowd, the newly updated liquid-cooled Himalayan 450 offers a rugged, tractor-like capability that can comfortably handle bad roads, dirt trails, and daily commutes without complaining. It’s an honest, unpretentious brand that focuses entirely on the pure joy of a simple ride.
Official Site: www.royalenfield.com
15Benelli

Benelli occupies a fascinating space in today's market. Founded in Italy over a century ago, the brand is now owned by China's Qianjiang (QJMOTOR) group. The design work still happens in Italy, giving bikes like the TRK 502 / 702 adventure series and the Leoncino scramblers a distinct, sharp Euro look, while the massive manufacturing power of China keeps the price tag incredibly low.

Purists sometimes grumble that they miss the old, temperamental Italian three-cylinder superbikes of Benelli’s past, but the reality is that their modern parallel-twin middleweights offer huge value for budget-conscious riders who want European street presence without paying premium European prices.
Official Site: www.benelli.com
16Bajaj

You might not see many Bajaj badges on highways in the United States or Western Europe, but make no mistake: this is a global manufacturing superpower. Based in India, Bajaj builds millions of small-to-medium displacement commuter bikes every single year that keep the economies of developing nations moving.

Their flagship Pulsar series is a massive icon across Asia and Latin America. Why are they on this list? Because they are the ultimate masters of small-displacement thermal efficiency and durability. Furthermore, Bajaj owns a massive 48% stake in KTM, meaning they are the actual engineering muscle responsible for building the highly popular, entry-level KTM Duke 200 and 390 platforms that riders love worldwide.
Official Site: www.bajajauto.com
17Norton

Norton is one of the grand historical pillars of British motorcycling, famous for the legendary "Featherbed" frame and the iconic Commando series. After a disastrous decade of financial mismanagement by previous British owners, the brand was rescued and bought outright by India's TVS Motor Company, who poured millions into building a state-of-the-art facility in Solihull.

Today, Norton is operating as a high-end, boutique luxury brand. They are carefully re-engineering classics like the Commando 961 and the breathtaking, carbon-fiber V4SV superbike to absolute perfection, focusing on flawless hand-welded frames, premium components, and bespoke British heritage. It’s an exclusive, old-school gentleman’s brand for those who value exclusivity and history above mass production.
Official Site: www.cagiva.it
18CFMOTO

If you want to watch a brand completely disrupt the global motorcycle establishment in real time, look at CFMOTO. While older riders might still be skeptical of Chinese manufacturers, CFMOTO has completely shattered expectations through a massive, tight technical partnership with KTM.

They aren't building cheap clones; they are building highly competitive, aggressive machines loaded with premium tech like big TFT displays, smartphone connectivity, and premium Brembo brakes. Middleweight sportbikes like the 450SS (450SR) are dominating lightweight racing classes thanks to their punchy 270-degree parallel-twin motors, while their Ibex 800 adventure tourers use proven KTM powerplant designs to deliver serious long-haul capability at a price that leaves Japanese and European rivals sweating. They are fast, they look incredible, and they are the biggest wild card in the industry right now.
Official Site: www.cfmoto.com
19Bimota

Bimota is the ultimate mad-science laboratory of the Italian exotic scene. Founded in Rimini, the company's entire historical blueprint consists of taking insanely powerful, reliable Japanese engines and dropping them into radical, custom-engineered Italian chassis that look like science fiction.

Now partially owned by Kawasaki, Bimota is producing low-volume, hyper-expensive unicorns like the Tesi H2. It takes the terrifying, supercharged 240-horsepower motor from the Kawasaki Ninja H2 and fits it into a chassis featuring a radical hub-center steering system instead of traditional front forks. It looks alien, it eliminates front-end dive under heavy braking, and it costs more than a luxury sports car. It is an elite badge reserved for collectors and engineering purists who want the rarest machinery money can buy.
Official Site: www.bimota.it
20Hero

Closing out the lineup is Hero MotoCorp, the single largest two-wheeler manufacturer in the entire world by volume. Based in India, Hero is the absolute king of mass mobility, building incredibly rugged, efficient, small-displacement workhorses like the Splendor that millions of people rely on for daily transport.

While they built their empire on basic commuters, Hero has recently been flexing its engineering muscle by partnering with Harley-Davidson to co-develop and manufacture the entry-level Harley X440, alongside launching their own highly capable, lightweight dual-sport adventure bike, the XPulse 200. They are the quiet titan of the industry, proving that sometimes the best brand isn't the one that goes the fastest, but the one that puts the entire world on wheels.
Official Site: www.heromotocorp.com
Wrapping It Up: How to Choose Your Ride

How do you even pick the right motorcycle? It's not really about how much power it has or how good the commercials are. It's more about finding a brand that just feels like it's for you. All these companies have spent many years creating their own distinct style.

If you want a bike that just works and always starts up easily, then you'd probably check out Japanese brands like Honda or Suzuki. But if you're looking for bikes with a lot of personality, great looks, and really wild performance, then Italian and Austrian brands like Ducati, Aprilia, or KTM are your go-to. They might cost a lot to keep running, but you'll love every minute of it.

Then there are brands like Harley-Davidson and Indian, famous for their classic cruiser style, which are perfect for riding on open roads. Older names like Triumph and Royal Enfield show that old-fashioned looks can still be great on bikes you can easily use daily. And if you're wondering what's next in motorcycles, companies like CFMOTO show how fast things are changing globally, bringing out new technology that even the legacy companies are paying attention to.

There's no such thing as a single best motorcycle brand. It's really about finding the bike that makes you want to go out, ride, and clear your head for a bit. Just think about the kind of rider you want to be, enjoy the engineering under the gas tank, and then just ride.
